summary: Reports on the second Coordinating Attack Response at Internet Scale (CARIS) workshop, sponsored by the Internet Society and held in Cambridge, Massachusetts in early 2019. Participants from incident response teams, operators, and service providers discussed how to coordinate responses to large-scale attacks. It is a workshop report, not a protocol specification.

eli5.summary: Experts who defend the Internet from attacks met to talk about how to team up faster, and this is the written record of what they discussed.

questions: how can incident response scale at internet scale
what protocols are used for incident response
how does encryption affect attack detection
subtitle: Report from a 2019 workshop on coordinating Internet-scale incident response.

tldr.problem: As Internet threats grow larger and encryption becomes ubiquitous, attack prevention and response becomes harder to coordinate across organizations, teams, and countries. There is no clear standard approach.
tldr.mechanism: The second CARIS workshop brought together incident responders, network operators, researchers, and vendors to discuss how to improve detection, prevention, and coordination when most Internet traffic is encrypted and unreadable.
tldr.outcome: The workshop identified five major research directions: standardization and adoption patterns, preventative protocols at scale, incident response coordination, monitoring and measurement, and common vocabularies for discussing threats.

today: RFC 8953 is an Informational document published in December 2020 reporting on a workshop held in 2019. It represents a snapshot of security research priorities at the time and documents community consensus on challenges in Internet incident response coordination. The research ideas proposed in the workshop remain relevant as encryption continues to expand across the Internet.

sections.title: The CARIS2 Workshop
sections.content:
On 28 February and 1 March 2019, the Internet Society sponsored the second Coordinating Attack Response at Internet Scale (CARIS2) workshop in Cambridge, Massachusetts. CARIS2 brought together 50+ participants: regional and national Computer Security Incident Response Teams (CSIRTs), network operators, service providers, security researchers, vendors, and standards community members. The workshop focused on a critical challenge: as the Internet shifts to strong encryption (TLS 1.3, QUIC, tcpcrypt), traditional network-based monitoring becomes impossible, yet organizations still need to detect and respond to attacks.

This was the second CARIS workshop. The first, held in 2017 (RFC 8073), started this conversation. CARIS2 continued that work with a focus on prevention and detection in an encrypted world, and on identifying research opportunities for a proposed new Internet Research Task Force (IRTF) research group on malware and threat research.
sections.eli5: Internet security experts held a two-day meeting to figure out how to spot attacks when you cannot see the network traffic because it is all encrypted.

sections.title: The Problem and Goals
sections.content:
The workshop was motivated by two realities. First, the global cybersecurity workforce is short by approximately three million people; training alone cannot fill the gap. Second, the Internet is moving to ubiquitous encryption, which protects user privacy but makes it much harder for defenders to see what is happening on the network wire.

The workshop had two main goals. The first was to scale attack response in an encrypted world: identify ways to prevent attacks and detect threats when encryption hides the content. The second was to seed a research agenda for the proposed SMART (Stopping Malware and Researching Threats) Research Group by identifying promising research ideas and communities that could explore them.

The organizers designed the workshop to foster collaboration between groups (incident responders, operators, researchers, vendors) who do not typically work together, reasoning that better coordination and shared insights across these groups could improve everyone's ability to detect and respond at scale.
sections.eli5: The goal was to figure out how to: (1) spot attacks when the network is encrypted, and (2) help different security teams work better together to fight big threats.

sections.title: Workshop Breakout Sessions and Findings
sections.content:
The workshop used five focused breakout sessions. The first, Standardization and Adoption, analyzed which security standards succeeded and which failed. TLS, SNMP, X.509, and IPFIX achieved wide adoption because they solved clear problems, had clean designs, and had early market-moving factors (e-commerce for TLS, vendor support for SNMP). Standards like STIX, IODEF, DANE, and IPv6 achieved only limited adoption despite being technically sound. The reasons ranged from too many dependencies (DANE requires DNSSEC) to unclear end-users (IPv6 was for "everyone", which meant no one in particular) to trust and privacy concerns (IODEF and STIX both face sharing reluctance).

The second breakout, Preventative Protocols and Scaling Defense, focused on automation. The group discussed the Manufacturer Usage Description (MUD) protocol for IoT device filtering, privacy-preserving Server Name Indication encryption, trust exchange mechanisms, and richer formats for sharing threat indicators (like the MISP platform used in Europe). A key insight: incident responders want to be involved early in protocol design to assess security and privacy implications.

The third session, Incident Response Coordination, identified what helps and what hinders incident response at scale. What helps: trust between incident responders, automated detection, legal and regulatory pressure to stay on top. What hinders: too many overlapping standards, unclear metrics, regulatory barriers to sharing, lack of skilled analysts, and reactionary approaches. Looming problems include government regulation, bifurcation of the Internet, and increasing centralization.

The fourth breakout, Monitoring and Measurement, proposed four research ideas. IP Address Reputation: create a database of IPv6 address lifetime and prefix characteristics so responders can better apply access controls without blocking legitimate traffic. SNARC (Server Name Authentication Reputation C): a mechanism to assign trust values to servers and clients for better threat detection. Logging at Compile Time: inject logging capabilities during application compilation for more uniform and consistent log data as encryption makes wire inspection impossible. Fingerprinting: identify malicious traffic patterns without decryption, while respecting privacy.

The fifth session discussed Taxonomies and Gaps. The group determined that a single universal taxonomy is not the answer; instead, tools to map between different taxonomies are needed because different groups (management, analysts, responders) need different levels of detail. A common vocabulary for discussing threats is more important than a rigid taxonomy.
sections.eli5: The groups talked about which security standards work (TLS works, IPv6 struggled), how to prevent attacks (encrypt more, automate responses), what stops incident responders (lack of trust, too many rules, shortage of experts), how to measure attacks while protecting privacy, and what words everyone should use to talk about threats.

sections.title: Key Research Ideas
sections.content:
Five research projects emerged with strong participant interest. Traffic Fingerprinting aims to identify malicious traffic by analyzing patterns (packet sizes, timing, flow characteristics) without reading the encrypted content. The challenge is balancing security benefits against privacy risks. SNARC proposes a system to score the trustworthiness of servers and clients to support zero-trust security models. Attack Coordination and Automated Security would develop better ways for incident responders and automated systems to work together to mitigate large-scale attacks. Cryptographic Rendezvous explores ways to encrypt sensitive information (like Server Name Indication) while still allowing legitimate monitoring. L2 Discovery works to prevent information leakage when devices reveal themselves through unencrypted Layer 2 protocols like DHCP.

Each of these efforts requires further development and community-building. The workshop helped establish connections and identify volunteer lead contacts for each project to drive progress.
sections.eli5: The five biggest ideas were: (1) spot bad traffic by its shape, not its content; (2) score how trustworthy a server is; (3) help different security teams attack big problems together; (4) hide sensitive info from the network but keep legitimate monitors happy; (5) fix the problem where devices leak secrets by accident.

sections.title: Challenges and Next Steps
sections.content:
The workshop revealed deep structural challenges. Incident response does not scale today and faces headwinds from regulatory complexity, regional data flow restrictions, and the shortage of trained analysts. Organizations are also struggling with a disconnect between perceived and actual risk, making it hard to prioritize response efforts.

Standards and protocols alone are not enough; adoption depends on factors like simplicity, clear incentives, market pressure, and early community involvement. Even well-designed standards (DANE, IODEF) can languish without these supporting factors. The workshop highlighted that privacy and security goals are sometimes in tension: monitoring, measurement, and threat detection often require data that privacy advocates want to protect. Balancing these requires early collaboration between security and privacy communities.

The workshop identified two next steps: (1) continue developing the research initiatives spawned by CARIS2, creating communities around each project and reporting progress to the SMART research group, and (2) plan for a future CARIS workshop to continue this conversation as the Internet evolves.
sections.eli5: The big takeaway: it is hard to fight attacks when you have to respect privacy and follow many different rules. The workshop found five promising ideas worth exploring and plans to keep talking about this in future meetings.

viz.caption: Five breakout session themes and what they addressed.

items.title: Standardization
items.text: Why TLS, SNMP, and IPFIX succeeded while DANE, STIX, and IPv6 struggled.

items.title: Prevention
items.text: Automating security controls and using protocols like MUD and encrypted SNI.

items.title: Coordination
items.text: What helps and hinders incident response: trust, automation, legal pressure, and too many standards.

items.title: Monitoring
items.text: IP reputation, trust scoring, better logging, and traffic fingerprinting without decryption.

items.title: Vocabulary
items.text: One taxonomy does not fit all; need mappings between taxonomies and common terms for threats.

items.title: Next Steps
items.text: Develop five research projects (fingerprinting, SNARC, coordination, cryptographic rendezvous, L2 discovery).
